title: How do you stop yourself from adding more and more
author: BallKnower_game
selftext:
It’s hard for me to stop myself from adding more systems, more mechanics, more aesthetic refinement. When the tools are so readily available and everything moves so efficiently, how do you say “enough”?

The other day I was playing and i remembered how old games used to have secret movement mechanics that only high skill players would master and eventually became meta. I couldn’t stop myself from adding that.

I was listening to Hypertrance, and i couldn’t help but think about how good it would feel playing in the back in combination with my movement. 

I played Straftat with friends and couldn’t stop wondering how to capture that feeling of flow in between rounds and how easy it is to pick up and put down.

Where do you stop?

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body: umm, write a GDD and don't change it later?

replies.author: BallKnower_game
replies.body: unfortunately i keep doing that. the base and core pillars stay the same, which is good, but i keep expanding upon them and have plans for even bigger things. i’m trying to keep it chill by separating into release “versions” ie 1.0, 2.0, 3.0. that way i keep track of what ABSOLUTELY has to be done.

replies.author: Square-Yam-3772
replies.body: you can also just give yourself a timeline i.e. release the game by this time. When you reach the date, release the game as is (version 1.2999 w/e) and then keep working on it

comments.author: Hawk_Vision_Games
comments.body:
The realization, that I want to ship a product and get players to play something new and interesting.  My current project I wanted to finish within a year, but I ran into this problem where I kept on adding more because I want it to be successful.  But after playing some of the "Friend Slop" games that had even less than what I ended-up making.  I realized I could probably just finish cleaning things up and button it up to see how it does.

You can always add more, as long as your games polished and fun.  People will be excited to see what updates you add later.  So adding more, unless it's critical to the project doesn't matter if no one else has played it to give that feedback.

comments.author: daddy_reloaded
comments.body: At one point I start to be overwhelmed by the features in my game, and then conducting a proper test plan (human one) becomes too difficult. This where I stop in general.

comments.author: Key-Media-6395
comments.body: honestly having the same problem. just got to not do it i guess

comments.author: Pixeltoir
comments.body:
Welcome to Game Dev!!!

Now you realize why most devs even before AI were unable to release their games

replies.author: BallKnower_game
replies.body: i feel like i was pretty good at managing this before ai because i had a baseline knowledge of my limitations, but with the new models and this being my first time using them for this purpose, it gets trickier. i guess i’ll figure out my limits when crash head first into them.

comments.author: Fuzzzy420
comments.body: Polish what you have until there is no more to polish, then continue adding stuff

replies.author: Raging_Rob
replies.body: this. polishing takes a lot of effort and if you just keep adding stuff you'll very quickly end up with a mess and essentially be forced to slow down if you want to make something worth playing

comments.author: XombiePrwn
comments.body:
Feature creep. Refine existing mechanics, rules, themes, graphics etc until they're fit for purpose. Once the underlying structure is there adding more is easier, if you/ the ai set a clear gamedev structure. I'm a noob btw, feature creep is something you account for early for easy implementation or sideline and account for later dev time hoping things don't break.

Happy to be wrong here.

comments.author: Nandor89
comments.body: For me the sweet spot is before you get bored to play your own prototype, play it again and again and you’ll see what is superfluous and what is really fun

comments.author: Individual_Solid_944
comments.body:
For most of the projects that I do, I would usually spend a good amount of time writing GDD, and a full specification. Then I review everything, make sure it's what I want. I may split some things, like whether things should go in v1.0 or later, so I can reduce the scope for the initial version. Well, not only that, but sometimes I would have a larger split for a PoC. And after double-checking everything and making sure everything is well specified, I would start development and not drift away. That's the guardrail to make sure I eventually ship.

This has been working really well for many years. Nowadays, as you say, things can move faster. And if you think about AI, sure, it may speed things up. But I try to keep things constrained, because if I ask an AI to draft my specification or GDD, it may blow it up, add things I don't even need and do all kinds of weird things. So, I do that part myself. Once I am done, I may pass it to an AI to check things out in order to find something I've missed, but I wouldn't let it edit those things for me. And I don't take it's advice for granted. I cherrypick the suggestions.

Aside from that discipline, I started making a game about 6 years ago. I did the process that I described, but without the rule to have clear guardrails. I thought I would do it when I have time, so like a couple of hours per day, but I would release when it's really done the way I want and really polished in every way, including mechanics, progression, visuals, sounds, you name it. It's been in a really good shape for a couple of years, and I still keep polishing the thing. It seems it will never be done really perfectly. And since I started I have spent at least 4 hours every day, and very often a lot more. The problem is I treat it as a hobby project, so I keep adding stuff. And when I release it, I won't be surprised if it doesn't succeed, despite all the effort. That's how this works, and I have published so many games, so I know this for a fact.

Well, as they say, this is a journey, not a destination.  
So if you want to ship, plant a flag before you even start, so you know where to go.  
And once there, publish. Then the community will tell you the direction, if you manage to get some.

comments.author: UncleJoesLandscaping
comments.body: I would seldom worry about adding too much polish unless its delaying the game a lot. Feature creep is a much bigger issue since it can often make the game objectively worse. Both because it makes the game more cluttery and because you wont be able to make everything as polished.

comments.author: PositiveScarcity8909
comments.body: Why would I add more stuff when I have to redo the characters 3 times from scratch so they don't look like slop.

comments.author: Upbeat-Mail7201
comments.body: Making a Game Design Document beforehand and spending more time planning the game is crucial, as planning often takes longer than execution. I spent about 2 years planning my game with a team, testing mechanics in a Python web demo before implementation. It's important to avoid feature creep and focus on making a few mechanics very good rather than many mediocre ones. Always consider if a feature enhances the game, adds fun, or creates emotion; if not, it may be unnecessary. Aim to perfect core mechanics first, with the option to add or cut features later.

comments.author: Brilliant_Feed4158
comments.body: I at some point started thinking: will this really add something to the game?

comments.author: BallKnower_game
comments.body: yes. 1.0 is ready to be released as is. 2.0 is mostly game modes and polish and multiplayer.

comments.author: dantemp
comments.body: I mean if you are doing solo dev on your own dime with no promises made to anyone, why shouldn't you?

comments.author: spoollyger
comments.body: Make the game fun. If it’s not fun, stop randomly adding more system.

comments.author: Ok-Sea300
comments.body: Pin new features for post release updates. It also helps the players see the game wasnt abandoned

comments.author: SeasawPhilosopher
comments.body:
You need to cultivate a very strong vision of what you want to build and set an extremely high bar for inclusion of new stuff. Everything you want to add you should be thinking very hard if it fits YOUR vision or if it’s just glueing a bunch of random fun ideas together. This is part of the human judgement side of AI dev that most people are actually not very good at and it’s how you can maintain a competitive advantage.

Also get good at removing stuff. If you are never willing to delete stuff from Yyour game it will inevitably become bloated over time. Nothing is precious. Anything that doesn’t earn its weight should get canned even if it took effort to make.

comments.author: Academic-Bench-8828
comments.body: I actually like games with overdone systems like factorio. So I'm biased first of all. I like having lots of systems but I think that the biggest problem is that most games kind of dump it all on you at once. Factorio did a good job of doling out small bits of complexity over time so you don't get too overwhelmed.
